Input formats

Written by Mohammed Saqr and Sonsoles López-Pernas

Source: vignettes/articles/input-formats.Rmd
input-formats.Rmd

A heterogeneous transition network needs two pieces of information that ordinary event logs store in different ways: the order of the coded events within each session, and the actor type that owns each code. Some studies keep one table per actor, because the two streams were coded separately (the messages of a learner and the replies of a chatbot, for example); others keep one table of all events with a column naming the actor; and others keep the events in one table and the coding scheme, which assigns every code to an actor, in a codebook. The analysis should not depend on which of these layouts the data happen to arrive in.

build_htna() accepts all three layouts and resolves them to the same interleaved sequence per session, so the resulting networks are identical. This guide shows each layout on the bundled data, verifies that they give the same network, and then covers two arguments that work with any layout: disambiguate, for a code label used by more than one actor, and group, for one network per cohort of sessions. Fitted clustering results are a fourth kind of input, covered in Clustering inputs.

library(htna)

Data

The package ships the same vibe-coding sessions (429 sessions of human-AI pair programming) in the three layouts.

  • human_simplified, ai_simplified: one long table per actor; each row is one coded event of that actor.
  • human_ai: both tables stacked, with the actor in actor_type ("Human" or "AI") and a session-level cohort tag phase ("Early", "Late").
  • human_ai_codebook: the coding scheme, one row per code, with columns code and actor_type.

All tables share the columns build_htna() reads by default:

  • Session: session_id (argument session).
  • Code: code (argument action).
  • Order: order_in_session (argument order), a time index shared by both actors within a session, so the two streams interleave in the order in which the events happened.
data(human_ai, human_simplified, ai_simplified, human_ai_codebook)
human_ai_codebook
#>         code actor_type
#> 1    Specify      Human
#> 2    Request      Human
#> 3  Frustrate      Human
#> 4      Check      Human
#> 5    Inquire      Human
#> 6     Refine      Human
#> 7   Delegate         AI
#> 8       Plan         AI
#> 9    Execute         AI
#> 10       Ask         AI
#> 11    Repair         AI
#> 12    Report         AI

The codebook assigns six codes to each actor: the human specifies, requests, checks, inquires, refines and expresses frustration; the AI delegates, plans, executes, asks, repairs and reports.

One table per actor

When each actor’s events are in a separate table, the tables are passed as a named list. The names become the actor types, in the order given.

net_list <- build_htna(list(Human = human_simplified, AI = ai_simplified))
summary(net_list)
#> <htna network>
#>   Method:    relative
#>   Sessions:  429   (max 287 timesteps)
#>   Nodes:     12
#>   Edges:     135 / 144 (non-zero)
#> 
#> Actor types (2):
#>   Human (6 nodes):  Check, Frustrate, Inquire, Refine, Request, Specify
#>   AI    (6 nodes):  Ask, Delegate, Execute, Plan, Repair, Report
#> 
#> Edge counts by actor (rows = source, cols = target):
#>           Human    AI
#>   Human      35    36
#>   AI         36    28
#> 
#> Network metrics:
#>                       metric    value
#>                   Node Count  12.0000
#>                   Edge Count 135.0000
#>              Network Density   1.0000
#>                Mean Distance   0.0274
#>            Mean Out-Strength   1.0000
#>              SD Out-Strength   0.0000
#>             Mean In-Strength   1.0000
#>               SD In-Strength   0.6309
#>              Mean Out-Degree  11.2500
#>                SD Out-Degree   0.9653
#>  Centralization (Out-Degree)   0.0579
#>   Centralization (In-Degree)   0.0579
#>                  Reciprocity   0.9600

The network has 12 nodes, six per actor, built from 429 sessions. Of the 144 possible directed edges 135 are non-zero, and the edge counts by actor show that transitions occur in every block: 35 within the human codes, 36 from human to AI, 36 from AI to human and 28 within the AI codes.

One table with an actor column

When all events are in one table, the column that names the actor of each row is passed as actor_type. The actor order follows the levels of that column if it is a factor, and the order of first appearance otherwise.

net_actor_type <- build_htna(human_ai, actor_type = "actor_type")

One table and a codebook

When the event table has no actor column, the assignment of codes to actors is declared with node_groups, either as a named list of codes or as a two-column codebook whose code column is named like action (here code).

net_codes <- build_htna(
  human_ai,
  node_groups = list(
    Human = c("Specify", "Request", "Frustrate", "Check", "Inquire", "Refine"),
    AI    = c("Delegate", "Plan", "Execute", "Ask", "Repair", "Report")
  )
)
net_codebook <- build_htna(human_ai, node_groups = human_ai_codebook)

A code in the data that is missing from node_groups, or listed under two actors, raises an error, so the declared scheme is checked against the data.

Do the layouts give the same network?

The edge table of a network (as.data.frame()) lists every non-zero transition with its weight and the actors of its two codes. If the four networks agree, their edge tables are equal.

edges_list <- as.data.frame(net_list)
all.equal(edges_list, as.data.frame(net_actor_type))
#> [1] TRUE
all.equal(edges_list, as.data.frame(net_codes))
#> [1] TRUE
all.equal(edges_list, as.data.frame(net_codebook))
#> [1] TRUE

All three comparisons return TRUE: the 135 edges, their weights and their actor assignments are the same whichever layout the data came in. The choice of layout is therefore a matter of how the data are stored, not of the analysis. A named list of networks is drawn one network per element:

op <- par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(1, 1, 3, 1))
plot_htna(list(list = net_list, actor_type = net_actor_type,
               node_groups = net_codes, codebook = net_codebook))

par(op)

The four panels are indistinguishable, as the edge tables predicted.

What if two actors use the same code label?

Some coding schemes give the same label to a move of either actor, for example Ask for a question from the human and a clarification request from the AI. Such codes are different behaviours, and merging them into one node would mix the two actors. build_htna() therefore stops when a label occurs under more than one actor. The small table below has Ask and Reply for both actors in each of three sessions.

overlap <- data.frame(
  session_id       = rep(c("s1", "s2", "s3"), each = 6),
  code             = rep(c("Ask", "Reply", "Ask", "Reply", "Ask", "Reply"), 3),
  actor_type       = rep(c("Human", "Human", "AI", "AI", "Human", "AI"), 3),
  order_in_session = rep(seq_len(6), 3)
)

Building the network as usual raises an error of class htna_actor_conflict that names the shared labels.

build_htna(overlap, actor_type = "actor_type")
#> Error:
#> ! Code(s) appear in more than one actor group: Ask, Reply. Pass `disambiguate = TRUE` to prefix codes with the actor label.

With disambiguate = TRUE every code is prefixed with its actor, so the two Ask codes become the separate nodes Human:Ask and AI:Ask.

net_dis <- build_htna(overlap, actor_type = "actor_type",
                      disambiguate = TRUE)
as.data.frame(net_dis, what = "nodes")
#>          node actor
#> 1      AI:Ask    AI
#> 2    AI:Reply    AI
#> 3   Human:Ask Human
#> 4 Human:Reply Human

The network has four nodes, two per actor, and each keeps its actor type.

How is one network built per cohort?

Any layout can be split into one network per cohort of sessions with group, which names a session-level column. human_ai has the column phase, which places the first 214 sessions in chronological order in Early and the remaining 215 in Late. The result is a grouped network (an htna_group) whose cohorts follow the factor levels of phase.

grp <- build_htna(human_ai, actor_type = "actor_type", group = "phase")
as.data.frame(summary(grp), what = "actor_pairs")
#>   group source_actor target_actor n_edges
#> 1 Early        Human        Human      35
#> 2 Early        Human           AI      36
#> 3 Early           AI        Human      36
#> 4 Early           AI           AI      28
#> 5  Late        Human        Human      35
#> 6  Late        Human           AI      36
#> 7  Late           AI        Human      36
#> 8  Late           AI           AI      27

Both cohorts have the same actor partition; the early network has 28 non-zero AI-to-AI edges and the late network 27, and the other blocks have the same counts in both. A grouped network is passed as it is to the other functions (plot_htna(), bootstrap_htna(), permutation_htna(), compare_htna() and the rest), which work through its cohorts. The Grouped heterogeneous transition networks vignette and the Comparing networks guide continue from here.

op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(1, 1, 3, 1))
plot_htna(grp)

par(op)

Which layout to use

Data at hand Call
One table per actor build_htna(list(Human = h, AI = a))
One table with an actor column build_htna(d, actor_type = "actor_type")
One table and a codebook build_htna(d, node_groups = codebook)
One table and code lists build_htna(d, node_groups = list(Human = ..., AI = ...))
A fitted clustering of sessions build_htna(fit); see Clustering inputs
A label shared by two actors add disambiguate = TRUE
One network per cohort add group = "phase"
